studies.title: Fed Against Hunger, Secured From Fear
studies.meaning: The whole chapter is one sentence, and its main clause does not arrive until the third line. It opens on a preposition, so the sense runs: because of the bonding of Quraysh, their bonding for the winter and summer journeys, let them worship the Lord of this House. Commentators differ over the opening word itself, reading it as a settled custom, as the agreements that made the roads safe, or as the attachment that held the tribe together. Then the reason is given in two halves, food against hunger and safety against fear.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Mecca grew nothing. Its position beside the sanctuary let its people live by trade rather than by farming, and safe passage was negotiated with the tribes along the routes: south toward the Yemen in winter, north toward Syria in summer. Classical sources report that these arrangements were formalised a generation or two before the mission, which is why the surah can speak of them as long familiar.

keyTerms.note: From a root of becoming familiar and attached. It covers a settled habit, a formal agreement, and affection between people, and the commentators keep all three, since the trade rested on every one of them at once.
The noun for mounting up and departing, formed from the word for a camel saddle. It names the leaving rather than the destination, so the two seasons are identified by the act of going.
From the root of safety, which is also the root of the word for believing. The two gifts named in this line, food and security, are therefore described in vocabulary that belongs to trust.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nothing edible grew in the valley. Grain came up from the Yemen and the coastal plains, while oil, cloth and worked goods came down from the north. Two caravans a year kept the city fed, and each one had to pass through territory held by tribes who could simply have taken it. The whole of Mecca's prosperity was an arrangement rather than a resource, which is precisely what the chapter names.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the chapter is built on appears twice, in its first two lines, and nowhere else in the Quran. The surah also has no verb until its third line, so a quarter of it is a prepositional phrase held open before anything is stated. Classical commentators and reciters discuss whether it continues the chapter immediately before it, which would supply the missing opening.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument runs from a commercial fact straight to worship with no step in between, and that is the whole move. Prosperity that was obviously arranged by human negotiation, treaty by treaty over decades, is presented as something given. The giver is then named by the House rather than by an attribute, tying the trade to the sanctuary that made the city worth travelling to in the first place.

crossReferences.why: Points at the same fact, a secure sanctuary while people are seized from the land around it.
Answers the fear of losing that security, naming a safe place to which fruits are brought from everywhere.
Records Abraham's prayer over a valley with no crops, asking that its people be provided with fruits.

studies.applyIt: Work out where one thing on your table this morning actually came from, and how many separate people had to do their jobs properly for it to reach you. Stop when you get to five. The chapter's argument is that an arrangement this elaborate is still a gift, and the arithmetic makes that easier to feel than to be told.
